two_stage_design.understanding: STAGE 1 — Layman to article/section: first pick ALL layman words/phrases and fetch them into article-section format. Convert every layman expression into legal terms, then map legal terms to section(s) via Laya choice questions. STAGE 2 — Recheck inside the article section: after Stage 1 picks sections, RECHECK each picked section against ALL its relations in the graph — prerequisites, exclusions/not_for, related_sections, guardrails, court, and co-firing sections. Only after that recheck is the answer final. A section failing its recheck is DROPPED with a reason, not kept. Then the legal terms are interconnected across sections.
two_stage_design.stage1: Layman phrase (EN + Kannada) -> legal term -> section candidate(s), one Laya choice per decision node. Confidence gate first: if no issue can be picked with confidence, clarify/escalate instead of force-picking.
two_stage_design.stage2: For each candidate: divorce gate first, then prerequisite, exclusion, related-section, co-fire, guardrail, court, escalate — in that order (Lane 3 pipeline). Any prerequisite/exclusion failure DROPS the section with a reason. Conditional routes (HMA 24/25/26/27) are kept as 'conditional_future' only when the user asked for the full picture / all options; in a live claim they drop unless their prerequisite holds.
two_stage_design.fast_path: Root choice (1 forward pass) -> one choice per selected lane in parallel -> section-set node -> procedure node. No free-text generation for section selection.

guardrails.rajnesh_v_neha: Maintenance ONLY. NEVER cite for Stridhan, custody, residence or divorce.
guardrails.satish_chander_ahuja: Shared household / residence ONLY. NEVER cite for custody.
guardrails.residence_label: Right to reside in the SHARED HOUSEHOLD. NEVER call it 'tenancy rights'.
guardrails.court_selection: The graph picks the court (Family Court, Bengaluru for HMA matters; Magistrate for BNSS s.144 and PWDVA matters). NEVER ask the user to pick the court.
guardrails.divorce_gate: HMA s.13 / s.13B ONLY if divorce was asked. In the test case no divorce was asked, so they must NOT fire.
guardrails.birth_certificate: Registration of Births and Deaths Act 1969. NOT the Hindu Marriage Act.
guardrails.salary_slips: Ask husband's income / school fees / where husband lives now. Do NOT demand salary slips the user said she does not have.
guardrails.quantum: Section selection is high-confidence on the test facts; maintenance QUANTUM is low-confidence until husband's income is known — escalate quantum, not section selection. Never invent an amount.
guardrails.no_double_counting: Do not double-count the same maintenance under both PWDVA s.20 and BNSS s.144 / HMA ss.24-25. PWDVA s.20 is one canonical section, shared by the maintenance and residence lanes.

phrasebook_with_v2_fixes.design_understanding: Stage 1 (layman to article/section): the user speaks in layman words — e.g. 'my husband is not giving me money', 'he took my gold', 'they are throwing me out' — and Laya must first convert each such phrase into legal terms (maintenance / neglect to maintain, Stridhan / return of property, right to reside in the shared household, custody, domestic violence, divorce) and then, via a Laya choice question per phrase, map those legal terms to candidate sections from the verified list only. Stage 2 (recheck inside the article section): after Stage 1 picks sections, each picked section is rechecked against ALL of its relations inside that section — its prerequisites, its exclusions/not_for list, its related/co-firing sections, its guardrails and its court — and only sections that survive that recheck stay in the final answer. A section that fails recheck (for example HMA 24 with no HMA proceeding pending, HMA 13/13B when divorce was not asked for, Rajnesh v. Neha cited for Stridhan, Satish Chander Ahuja cited for custody, or residence labelled 'tenancy rights') must be DROPPED with a reason, not kept. Example rechecks built into this phrasebook: maintenance phrases recheck BNSS 144 against HMA 24 vs 25 and PWDVA 20 without double-counting; Stridhan phrases recheck HMA 27 together with BNS 316; custody phrases recheck the welfare-of-the-child principle overriding the HMGA s.6 natural-guardian default; residence phrases recheck PWDVA 17+18+19+20 as a set.

mappings_detail.design_understanding: Two-stage design confirmed. STAGE 1 (this file) — Layman -> legal term -> section: pick ALL layman words/phrases from the user's question, convert every layman expression into legal terms, then map each legal term to verified section(s) via Laya choice questions where the mapping is ambiguous. One layman sentence may raise 2-4 issues and must be split into separate legal terms, each mapped independently. Negations in Stage 1 BLOCK sections (e.g. 'no divorce' blocks HMA 13/13B and gates HMA 24/27 on a pending proceeding) before Stage 2 ever sees them. Out-of-scope layman questions must escalate, never be forced onto a section. STAGE 2 (lane 3) — Recheck inside the article section: after Stage 1 picks sections, RECHECK each picked section against ALL its relations (prerequisites, exclusions/not_for, related_sections, guardrails, court, co-firing sections). A section failing recheck (wrong issue, missing prerequisite, divorce not asked, etc.) must be DROPPED with a reason, not kept. Examples: BNSS 144 firing must recheck HMA 24 vs 25 and PWDVA 20; Stridhan must recheck HMA 27 + BNS 316 together; custody must recheck welfare-of-the-child overriding the natural-guardian default; residence must recheck PWDVA 17+18+19+20 as a set.

global_guardrails.rule: Rajnesh v. Neha (2021) 2 SCC 324 is maintenance ONLY (quantum criteria + affidavit of assets/liabilities). NEVER cite it for Stridhan, custody, residence or divorce.
Satish Chander Ahuja v. Sneha Ahuja (2020) is shared household / residence ONLY. NEVER cite it for custody, guardianship, natural guardianship or the welfare principle.
Residence is the right to reside in the SHARED HOUSEHOLD. NEVER call it 'tenancy rights'; the woman is not a tenant and no landlord-tenant relationship is created.

The graph picks the court — Family Court, Bengaluru for HMA matters; Judicial Magistrate First Class, Bengaluru for BNSS s.144 and PWDVA matters; criminal complaint / FIR route for BNS s.316. NEVER ask the user to pick the court.

NEVER demand the husband's salary slips — the user said she does not have them. ASK instead: husband's income (estimate/range), school fees of the 8yo daughter, where the husband lives now. Absence of salary slips is never a reason to refuse or delay a claim.

Maintenance QUANTUM is escalated, never invented. No amount may be stated without the husband's income and the parties' means; section selection may be high-confidence while quantum stays low-confidence.

Do not double-count the same maintenance under both PWDVA s.20 and BNSS s.144 / HMA ss.24-25. Amounts claimed under parallel routes are set off against each other; the same month's maintenance is recovered once.
The child's birth certificate is under the Registration of Births and Deaths Act 1969. NEVER say it is under the Hindu Marriage Act.

set_co_fire_rules.rule: BNSS 144 firing rechecks HMA 24 vs HMA 25 and PWDVA 20 as a set. HMA 24 is INTERIM (only while an HMA proceeding is pending); HMA 25 is PERMANENT (only at/after a decree); BNSS 144 is the subsistence route (no HMA proceeding needed); PWDVA 20 is monetary relief for domestic-violence consequences. State the interim-vs-permanent distinction explicitly every time more than one of these fires. Set off amounts across routes — never double-count the same month's maintenance.

Stridhan rechecks the civil return route + BNS 316 TOGETHER: BNS 316 (criminal) and the civil return route must be cited together — HMA 27 where an HMA proceeding is pending/being filed, otherwise the Family Court property suit under Family Courts Act s.7(1) Expl. (c) / CPC s.151; never cite BNS 316 as the civil recovery route by itself, and never cite HMA 27 without a proceeding. If no demand for return has been made yet, BNS 316 is NOT dropped — it goes to demand-first fallback: make a written demand / legal notice first, then re-evaluate BNS 316 (see bns-316 check R-BNS316-03).

Custody rechecks welfare-of-the-child OVER the natural-guardian default: for the 8yo daughter (above five) the father is the natural guardian under HMGA s.6, so the mother's custody claim rests on the welfare principle, which overrides the default natural-guardian order — never deny the father's status, never cite HMGA s.6 as granting custody by itself. HMA 26 is the route inside a pending HMA proceeding; GWA 1890 is the fallback/standalone route when no HMA proceeding exists; exactly one of HMA 26 / GWA 1890 is the primary custody route on any given facts.

Residence rechecks PWDVA 17+18+19+20 as a set: s.17 is the RIGHT to reside in the shared household (foundation); s.18 is the PROTECTION order stopping the threats/violence; s.19 is the enforceable RESIDENCE order (restraint on dispossession, removal, alternative accommodation/rent); s.20 is the MONEY (including rent for alternative accommodation if she cannot stay). Firing any one of ss.17/19 without rechecking the other three is a recheck failure.

sections.title: Restitution of conjugal rights
sections.when_used: When either spouse has, without reasonable excuse, withdrawn from the society of the other, and the aggrieved spouse wants the other to come back and resume living together as husband and wife — not a divorce, not maintenance alone. Bank question B-018: husband left home six months ago and refuses to return; wife wants him to come back, and needs money to run the house until then (maintenance meanwhile is BNSS s.144 / PWDVA s.20, not s.9 itself).
prerequisites: A valid marriage to which the HMA applies.
The respondent spouse has withdrawn from the society of the petitioner (stopped living together as husband and wife).
The withdrawal is without reasonable excuse — under the Explanation to s.9 the burden of proving reasonable excuse is on the person who withdrew.
The court is satisfied of the truth of the statements in the petition and that there is no legal ground why the application should not be granted (HMA s.9 read with s.23).
Petition to the District Court (Family Court where the Family Courts Act applies).
sections.court: Family Court, Bengaluru (District Court under HMA s.9; matrimonial petitions lie before the Family Court under the Family Courts Act, 1984). The graph picks the court — never ask the user to pick the court.
sections.relief: Decree for restitution of conjugal rights directing the respondent spouse to resume cohabitation. The decree does not compel physical cohabitation by force; if there is no restitution for one year or upwards after the decree, either party may seek divorce under HMA s.13(1A)(ii) — cite s.13 only if divorce is then asked for. Maintenance while separated is a separate claim (BNSS s.144 / PWDVA s.20); interim maintenance during the s.9 proceeding can be sought under HMA s.24.

laya_question.question: Has your spouse left home / withdrawn from living with you as husband and wife, without a reasonable excuse, and do you want them to come back and resume living together (rather than seeking a divorce)?
options: yes — spouse left / refuses to return, and I want them back
no — we are living together, or I do not want them back
unclear — whether they left, why, or what I want is not stated
laya_question.expected_answer_for_test_case: yes — spouse left six months ago, refuses to return, user wants him back
laya_question.confidence_basis: Brutal-bank question B-018 (C1): 'My husband left our home six months ago and refuses to return. I want him to come back, and until then I need money to run the house.' Second rater verified the hma-9 use as legitimate.

related_sections.relationship: Maintenance while separated: BNSS s.144 is the live immediate route for money to run the house until the spouse returns; s.9 itself orders return, not money.
Monetary reliefs while separated (expenses, household costs) can run alongside the s.9 petition where domestic violence / economic abuse is alleged.
Interim maintenance during the s.9 proceeding: HMA s.24 applies once the restitution petition is pending, for support and litigation expenses during the proceeding.
Fallback only: if there is no restitution for one year or upwards after a s.9 decree, divorce lies under HMA s.13(1A)(ii). Never cite s.13 unless divorce is expressly asked for.
Procedure: the s.9 petition is filed in the Family Court as an HMA matrimonial petition.

escalate_rule.condition: Escalate to a human lawyer / LLM review when confidence is low or any of the missing facts below is absent; do NOT guess whether the withdrawal had a reasonable excuse, and do NOT promise the spouse will return.
missing_facts: When and how the spouse left, and whether they refuse to return
Any reason the spouse gives for leaving — cruelty, dowry demands, violence or any other excuse claimed (the withdrawing spouse bears the burden of proving reasonable excuse)
Whether the petitioner wants reunion or is using s.9 only as a step towards divorce (if divorce is the real aim, s.9 is the wrong route)
Where the respondent spouse lives now (jurisdiction / service)
Whether any HMA proceeding is already pending
escalate_rule.on_missing: Ask for the missing facts once; if still missing, flag the section as 'provisional — withdrawal / excuse unconfirmed' and escalate rather than asserting restitution as established.

exclusions: NOT a divorce remedy — divorce is HMA ss.13/13B, cited only if divorce is expressly asked for.
NOT a maintenance remedy by itself — money while separated is BNSS s.144 / PWDVA s.20 (and HMA s.24 once a proceeding is pending).
NOT available where the withdrawal has a reasonable excuse (e.g. cruelty by the petitioner) — the excuse, if proved by the withdrawing spouse, defeats the petition.
NOT enforceable by forcing the spouses to live together — the decree directs resumption of cohabitation; non-compliance grounds divorce under s.13(1A)(ii) after one year.
NOT for spouses outside the HMA (other personal laws have their own restitution provisions, e.g. Special Marriage Act s.22).

sections.act: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 (PWDVA)
sections.title: Compensation orders
sections.when_used: When an aggrieved woman has suffered injuries — including mental torture and emotional distress — from acts of domestic violence, and wants the respondent to pay compensation and damages for those injuries, in addition to any other relief under the Act. Bank question B-019: husband broke her arm, she spent Rs 60,000 on hospital treatment, and wants him to pay her medical costs plus monthly support (medical costs = s.22 compensation; monthly support = PWDVA s.20 / BNSS s.144, not s.22).
prerequisites: Aggrieved woman (PWDVA s.2(a) — 'aggrieved person' is a woman) in a domestic relationship with the respondent.
Act(s) of domestic violence committed by the respondent.
Injuries caused by those acts — physical injury, and/or mental torture and emotional distress (expressly named in s.22).
Application by the aggrieved person, ordinarily within the application under PWDVA s.12, before the Magistrate.
sections.court: Judicial Magistrate First Class (Magistrate) under the PWDVA, on an application under PWDVA s.12. The graph picks the court — never ask the user to pick the court.
sections.relief: Order directing the respondent to pay compensation and damages for the injuries, including mental torture and emotional distress, caused by the acts of domestic violence. It is in addition to every other relief under the Act (protection s.18, residence s.19, monetary reliefs s.20, custody s.21) — never an either/or. There is no statutory tariff: quantum is assessed judicially on the injuries and losses proved (medical bills, nature and duration of injury, mental torture / emotional distress). Medical costs such as B-019's Rs 60,000 hospital bill are compensable as injury costs. Monthly support is NOT s.22 — that is PWDVA s.20 / BNSS s.144.

laya_question.question: Did the domestic violence cause you injuries — a physical injury, medical expenses, mental torture or emotional distress — and do you want the respondent to pay compensation / damages for those injuries?
options: yes — injuries / medical costs / mental torture from domestic violence, compensation wanted
no — no injury from violence, only maintenance / protection wanted
unclear — whether there was an injury or what it cost is not stated
laya_question.expected_answer_for_test_case: yes — broken arm, Rs 60,000 hospital treatment, compensation for medical costs wanted
laya_question.confidence_basis: Brutal-bank question B-019 (C1): 'My husband broke my arm and I spent 60,000 rupees on hospital treatment. I want him to pay my medical costs and monthly support.' Second rater verified the pwdva-22 use as legitimate.

related_sections.relationship: Protection: the violence that caused the injury is addressed by a s.18 protection order; s.22 then compensates the injury itself. Cite together where violence is ongoing or threatened.

Distinct money head: s.20 is monetary relief for expenses/losses and maintenance (including medical expenses as an expense head); s.22 is compensation/damages for the injury itself, in addition to s.20. Never double-count the same rupee under both heads — set off, never duplicate.
Residence lane: where the violence also drove the woman out of the shared household, s.19 residence relief runs alongside s.22 compensation.
Monthly support in B-019 is BNSS s.144 (with PWDVA s.20), not s.22: s.22 compensates the injury (one-off / assessed damages), s.144/s.20 provide the recurring monthly maintenance.
Procedure: the s.22 claim is made by application to the Magistrate under PWDVA s.12, ordinarily together with the other PWDVA reliefs.

escalate_rule.condition: Escalate to a human lawyer / LLM review when confidence is low or any of the missing facts below is absent; do NOT invent a compensation amount — there is no statutory tariff and quantum is judicially assessed.
missing_facts: Nature and extent of the injuries (what happened, when, medical record / hospital bills — e.g. the Rs 60,000 in B-019)
Mental torture / emotional distress facts, if compensation is claimed for those (what was done, duration, effect)
Whether compensation for the same injury has already been claimed in a civil suit (amounts paid under a civil decree are set off, not duplicated)
Respondent's capacity to pay (for the quantum actually recoverable)
Whether the violence is ongoing — if so, protection (s.18) is urgent alongside compensation
escalate_rule.on_missing: Ask for the missing facts once; if still missing, flag the section as 'provisional — injury / quantum unconfirmed' and escalate rather than asserting a compensation figure.
